**CNN Entertainment**

**Hugh Jackman unsheathes the claws again for 'X-Men Origins: Wolverine'**

*   **STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
    *   "X-Men Origins: Wolverine" opens in theaters nationwide on Friday, May 1.
    *   Hugh Jackman reprises his iconic role as the mutant superhero for a fourth time.
    *   Jackman and producer Lauren Shuler Donner talk with CNN about the grueling physical demands of the film's iconic "Weapon X" transformation scene.

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)** -- Summer movie season is officially upon us, and it’s kicking off with a sharp snikt. 

Nine years after he first put on the leather suit in 2000’s groundbreaking *X-Men*, Australian actor Hugh Jackman is back as Marvel's premier rage-fueled mutant in *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*. But this time, he’s going it alone. 

The prequel explores the elusive back-story of Logan—the man who would become Wolverine—tracing his path from 19th-century Canada through centuries of conflict alongside his dark-spirited brother, Victor Creed (Liev Schreiber), and ultimately into the hands of the secretive Weapon X program.

For comic book fans, the holy grail of Wolverine’s lore has always been the terrifying experiment that fuses the indestructible fictional metal, adamantium, to his skeleton. Translating the iconic scene—where a naked, submerged Logan erupts from a water tank with newfound claws—from the page to the big screen required months of planning, intense physical conditioning, and miles of waterproof wiring.

CNN’s Richard Alleyne sat down with star Hugh Jackman and longtime *X-Men* producer Lauren Shuler Donner to discuss the making of the film, and the torturous shoot behind Wolverine's dramatic rebirth.

***

### **TRANSCRIPT: Going inside the Weapon X Tank**

**CNN:** Hugh, fans have been waiting years to see the Adamantium bonding process on the big screen. It’s the definitive moment for this character. What was the physical reality of shooting that scene?

**HUGH JACKMAN:** [Laughs] The physical reality was mostly me being completely freezing cold, entirely naked, and submerged in a giant glass cylinder for about fourteen hours a day! No, seriously, it was intense. When we shot the original *X-Men*, we saw glimpses of the flash-backs—the needles, the water—but here, we had to deliver the full horror and beauty of that moment. 

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:** It was really the centerpiece of the whole production design. In the comics, Barry Windsor-Smith drew this incredible, iconic visual of Logan with the helmet and the tubes underwater. We wanted to honor that visual iconography while making it feel medically plausible—well, as plausible as bonding alien metal to a guy's bones can be!

**CNN:** Lauren, from a producer’s standpoint, what were the logistics of setting up that water-tank shoot?

**SHULER DONNER:** It was a nightmare in the best possible way! We built this massive, custom glass vat filled with hundreds of gallons of water. We had to pump in warm water so Hugh wouldn't get hypothermia, but warm water creates condensation on the glass, which ruins the shots. So our special effects team was constantly fighting steam, water pressure, and mechanical rigs submerged in water. Plus, we had dozens of real, thick cables attached to Hugh’s body.

**JACKMAN:** Yeah, let’s talk about those cables! [Laughs] I had these giant rubber tubes glued to my skin, and they were heavy. When you’re underwater, you’re trying to act like you are in absolute agony—which, frankly, didn't require much acting. The adamantium bonding is supposed to be the most painful thing a human being could ever survive. I had to hold my breath, burst out of the water, roar at the top of my lungs, and look like an absolute animal.

**CNN:** You were in incredible shape for this movie—arguably leaner and more muscular than in the previous three *X-Men* films. Did the tank scene dictate your physical regimen?

**JACKMAN:** 100 percent. I knew that when I burst out of that tank, there was nowhere to hide. No suit, no shadows. Just me, wet, screaming, and out of my mind with rage. I was waking up at 4:00 a.m. every day to do heavy weightlifting, followed by a strict high-protein diet. By the time we filmed the tank escape, I had been dehydrating myself for about 36 hours beforehand just to get that shredded, vascular look. I was terrified I’d faint in the water!

**SHULER DONNER:** Hugh is too modest. His dedication was terrifying. I remember looking at the monitor during his burst-out moment—when he hits the water glass, breaks out, and runs down the corridor into the forest—and thinking, "That isn't a Hollywood actor. That is genuinely a wild beast." 

**CNN:** Hugh, when you finally break out of the water and unsheathe the claws for the first time in that scene, it’s a huge cinematic payoff. How did it feel filming that dynamic exit?

**JACKMAN:** It was liberating! Literally! You’re underwater, holding your breath, holding all this tension inside, and then the director calls action, the explosions go off, the glass breaks, and you just let loose. I sprinted out of that tank, buck naked—sorry to the crew members on set that day—and popped the claws. It was pure adrenaline. 

**SHULER DONNER:** We actually had to digitally add a bit of smoke and water spray to keep the PG-13 rating intact during his escape, because Hugh was so fast, he outran our strategic camera angles! 

**JACKMAN:** [Laughs] Hey, when you've got giant drills coming at your head and you've just been injected with metal, you run fast! But honestly, to see that moment come together—to go from Logan the man to Wolverine the weapon—it’s the heart of the movie. I think fans are going to get a real kick out of it.

***

*X-Men Origins: Wolverine* opens in theaters nationwide Friday. The film is rated PG-13.

**CNN** — It remains one of the most viscerally memorable sequences in superhero cinema history: Logan, dripping with water, strapped with wires, and driven mad by pain, bursting out of an alkali tank with fresh adamantium fused to his bones. 

While 2009’s *X-Men Origins: Wolverine* received mixed reviews from critics, the "Weapon X" escape sequence remains a high watermark for comic book faithful adaptations. 

To mark the anniversary of the film, star Hugh Jackman and veteran *X-Men* franchise producer Lauren Shuler Donner sat down with CNN to reflect on the brutal shoot, the logistical nightmares of filming in a giant water tank, and the unexpected challenges of shooting an iconic action scene entirely naked.

*The following transcript has been edited for length and clarity.*

---

### 'We had to make it feel primal'

**CNN:** Take us back to the set in Sydney. When you looked at the storyboard for the Weapon X sequence, what was the primary goal?

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:** Well, if you know the comics — specifically Barry Windsor-Smith’s *Weapon X* arc from 1991 — that image of Logan breaking out of the tank with the helmet and the hoses is holy grail territory for fans. We knew we couldn’t soft-pedal it. It had to be bloody, it had to be painful, and it had to feel primal. 

**HUGH JACKMAN:** I remember looking at the schedule and seeing two full weeks dedicated just to the tank and the immediate hallway breakout. I thought, "Great, two weeks in a warm pool!" *(Laughs)* I was so wrong. It was freezing, I was dripping wet for 12 hours a day, and I had practically nothing on.

**DONNER:** Hugh is being modest. He was in peak physical condition, but keeping that physique while submerged in water for hours is dangerous. Your body temperature drops fast. We had heaters in the tank, but every time he burst out into the air, the chill set in immediately.

**JACKMAN:** The hardest part wasn't the cold, though. It was the mindset. Up until that point in the story, Logan is a man trying to suppress his animal instincts. The Weapon X procedure strips away his humanity entirely. I told Gavin [Hood, the director], "When I come out of that water, I shouldn't look like a superhero. I should look like a rabid dog that’s just been tortured."

---

### The logistics of a naked breakout

**CNN:** Hugh, that scene is famous not just for the action, but for the fact that you played the entire breakout completely nude. How did you navigate that on set?

**JACKMAN:** *(Laughs)* Oh, mate. That was a day. Look, in the comics, he’s wearing a battery pack, some straps, and that’s about it. So we tried doing takes with flesh-colored shorts, but in the water, they just looked... ridiculous. It ruined the illusion. So I turned to Gavin and Lauren and said, "Look, let's just clear the set."

**DONNER:** We had a completely closed set. Minimal crew, only essential personnel. But Hugh being Hugh, he wanted to do all his own stunts running down that hallway. 

**JACKMAN:** Right, so I burst out of the tank, screaming, claws out—which were practical props at the time, mind you, very sharp—and I’m sprinting down this metal corridor. On one take, I rounded a corner, and the ring of female crew members who weren't supposed to be there were standing right behind the camera. 

**DONNER:** I remember that! 

**JACKMAN:** I tried to cover up with my hands, forgot I had these nine-inch sharp steel blades attached to my knuckles, and accidentally sliced the inner part of my thigh. Didn't hit anything vital, thank God! But I was standing there, bleeding, completely naked, holding metal claws. That was the moment I realized, "I really love my job, but this is insane."

---

![Actor Hugh Jackman on set as Wolverine.](javascript:void(0)) 
*Hugh Jackman as Logan in 'X-Men Origins: Wolverine' (2009).* 20th Century Fox/Marvel

---

### Balancing practical effects with CGI

**CNN:** Visually, the scene holds up remarkably well. How much of what we see on screen was practical versus computer-generated?

**DONNER:** Almost all the water work was real. The tank was a massive structure built on a soundstage. The liquid was actually a dense, murky mixture of water and non-toxic theatrical gels to give it that heavy, chemical look. 

**JACKMAN:** The breathing apparatus was the tricky part. I actually had a regulator in my mouth under the water. The director would yell "Action," I’d spat the regulator out, float to the bottom, and then explode upward. The adrenaline was real because, frankly, you're holding your breath, underwater, blind because of the murky liquid, waiting for your cue.

**DONNER:** When he ruptures the glass and the water pours out into the lab—that was real water, thousands of gallons unleashed at once. You only get one or two takes with something like that because the reset takes an entire day.

**JACKMAN:** You can’t fake that look of sheer shock on the actors' faces playing the scientists. When that glass shattered, that was real pressure pushing against them.

---

### The scene's legacy in the Wolverine saga

**CNN:** That moment set the stage for how Wolverine was portrayed in later films, particularly *Logan* (2017) and *X-Men: Apocalypse* (2016), which briefly revisited the Weapon X facility. Looking back, how do you view that scene's place in your legacy with the character?

**DONNER:** I think it was the scene where Hugh truly unleashed the full rage of the character. Before that, in the original trilogy, he was tough, he was cool, but he was contained. Weapon X proved to the studio—and to the audience—that Wolverine was at his best when he was unfiltered and feral.

**JACKMAN:** It was a turning point for me as an actor with Logan. Up to then, I was playing a guy who was reluctant to fight. In that tank, he dies, and the weapon is born. It allowed us years later to push the envelope even further with *Logan* and, eventually, *Deadpool & Wolverine*. Whenever I need to find that deep, dark inner rage for the character, I still think back to being at the bottom of that freezing cold tank in Sydney, waiting to burst out.

The high-tech visual design of the tank, the fluid, the sheer horror of the procedure—we wanted it to feel visceral, painful, and deeply faithful to the books.

**HUGH JACKMAN:** It really felt like paying off a ten-year promise to the fans. In the previous films, Logan only has fuzzy memories of it. But here, the audience is right there in the water tank with him, experiencing the agony of having liquid metal fused to his bones. 

**INTERVIEWER:** Hugh, let’s talk about your physical transformation for this sequence, because you are in undeniably the best shape of your life here. You’ve mentioned looking outside the superhero genre for physique inspiration this time around?

**HUGH:** Yeah, absolutely. I didn’t just want to look big; I wanted Logan to look lean, terrifying, and borderline animalistic. I actually looked at Robert De Niro in *Cape Fear*. 

**INTERVIEWER:** De Niro in *Cape Fear*?

**HUGH:** Mate, go back and look at De Niro in that film! He wasn't just "built"—he had this insane, shredded, veiny look that made him look dangerous, like a coiled spring ready to snap. There was an edge to his physique. I told my trainer, "I don't want to look like a bodybuilder; I want to look like a guy who will tear your throat out." So we upped the anti-diet, did intense weight sessions at 4:00 AM every morning, and for the tank scene specifically, I did a 36-hour dehydration routine. 

**LAUREN:** Which was terrifying for us as producers! 

**HUGH:** [Laughs] 

**LAUREN:** I kept running around set going, "Get Hugh some water! Please don't let our lead actor pass out!" But honestly, when he stepped onto the set and got into that tank... the crew went dead silent. He looked like an anatomical drawing come to life. 

**INTERVIEWER:** Speaking of that tank—filming underwater scenes is notoriously difficult. I heard there were some unique communication issues while shooting the bonding sequence?

**HUGH:** [Starts laughing] Oh mate, the underwater direction was a nightmare!

**LAUREN:** Tell him about Gavin [Hood, the director].

**HUGH:** Okay, so I am submerged in a massive, freezing water tank. I’m wearing a harness, wired up with hoses, holding my breath, trying to act like I'm suffering the most intense physical trauma of my life. To give me direction, our director, Gavin Hood, had an underwater speaker rigged up so I could hear him while I was submerged. 

**INTERVIEWER:** How did that sound?

**HUGH:** It sounded like an angry whale! Gavin has this wonderful, intense South African accent, but underwater it was completely garbled. I’m holding my breath for ninety seconds, trying to give this deep, emotional performance, veins popping out of my neck, and all I hear through the water is: *"Glub-glub-HUGH-glub-MORE-RAGE-glub-NO-BUBBLES!"* 

**LAUREN:** [Laughs] "No bubbles" was the big mandate!

**HUGH:** Yes! Gavin pops up to the surface after a take and goes, "Hugh! That was brilliant, mate, incredible rage! But you’re breathing out through your nose! You’re releasing air bubbles, and the bubbles are refracting the laser lights!" So I’m standing there, freezing, completely dehydrated, trying to summon the primal fury of a mutant weapon, while obsessively monitoring my nostrils so I don't let out a single bubble. 

**LAUREN:** It was the ultimate test of acting—expressing absolute, wild savagery while maintaining total physical control underwater. 

**INTERVIEWER:** Well, seeing the final cut, all that breath-holding and dehydration clearly paid off. 

**HUGH:** Thanks, mate. I survived it! And honestly, the moment Logan bursts out of that water, claws popping for the first time with that fresh adamantium... every second of freezing water and zero carbs was totally worth it. 

**LAUREN:** It’s the definitive Wolverine moment. Fans are going to love it.

**INTERVIEWER:** Hugh, Lauren, thank you so much for your time. 

**HUGH:** Cheers, mate! Thank you.

**CNN —** It remains one of the most iconic—and painful-looking—moments in superhero cinema history. 

In 2009's *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*, fans finally saw the brutal live-action origin of Logan’s adamantium skeleton. Encased in a glass water tank, hooked up to breathing tubes and injected with molten metal, Hugh Jackman’s character undergoes a terrifying transformation before roaring to life and breaking free.

To mark the legacy of the franchise, CNN sat down with star Hugh Jackman and longtime *X-Men* franchise producer Lauren Shuler Donner to look back at what it took to film the infamous "Weapon X" tank sequence.

***

**CNN:** Take us back to that set. When you look at the blue-lit tank, the tubes, the water—what was the atmosphere like on day one of shooting that sequence?

**Lauren Shuler Donner:** High anxiety! *(Laughs)* From a producer's standpoint, whenever you put your main star in a enclosed tank filled with liquid, plugged into actual hoses, your stress levels go through the roof. Safety was step number one, two, and three.

**Hugh Jackman:** Oh, mate, it was intense. I remember walking onto the soundstage in Sydney, seeing this massive, glowing apparatus, and thinking, "Right, so I’m actually going in there." I was in peak physical condition, but nothing prepares you for spending eight hours a day pruned in a glass box. 

**CNN:** Hugh, how much of that scene was practical versus CGI? Because it feels very visceral.

**Jackman:** Almost all of the tank work was practical. I was in the water, holding my breath, wearing custom contact lenses so my eyes looked completely bloodshot and dilated. The breathing apparatus was real, though obviously modified so I could actually get oxygen between takes. But when Logan is thrashing around in agony as the adamantium binds to his bones? That wasn't much of an act. The water was warm at first, but after hours, you’re freezing, you’re prune-skinned, and you’re screaming underwater.

**Shuler Donner:** And let’s not forget the logistics of keeping it PG-13! Hugh was completely naked in that tank. 

**Jackman:** *(Laughs)* Extremely naked, Lauren.

**Shuler Donner:** Extremely naked. So, beyond the dramatic tension of the Weapon X program, my job in the editing room later was making sure we had enough bubbles, water refraction, and strategic angles so we didn't get slapped with an R rating before he even burst out of the facility.

```
[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Hugh Jackman as Wolverine submerged in the Weapon X tank in 2009's 'X-Men Origins: Wolverine']
```

**CNN:** Let's talk about the breakout moment. Logan flatlines, the scientists think he’s dead, and then he bursts out of the water, claws dripping, absolutely furious. What was filming that explosive exit like?

**Jackman:** That was pure adrenaline. We had air cannons in the tank to make the water explode upward when I popped out. I remember Director Gavin Hood telling me, "When you break that surface, I don't want a superhero. I want a hunted, wounded animal." I leapt out, landed on the slick tile floor, gave this massive primal roar... and immediately slipped and nearly wiped out because my feet were soaking wet.

**Shuler Donner:** But you stayed in character! You recovered so fast. That shot of him bursting out, water flying everywhere, popping the claws for the first time with the adamantium—it gave everyone on set chills. We knew right then that despite how tough the shoot was, we had captured the true essence of Wolverine's trauma.

**Jackman:** It’s a crucial moment for the character. It’s the exact second Logan dies and Wolverine is truly born. Looking back, despite the cold water and the prune fingers, it's one of my favorite sequences we ever put on film. 

***

*X-Men Origins: Wolverine is currently streaming on Disney+.*
